steps.title: In the ground

form.name: Host ore or residue
form.label: tens of grams of scandium a tonne

steps.text: Scandium is not rare, but it almost never concentrates. It is spread at tens of grams a tonne through nickel laterites, titanium and zirconium ores, bauxite residue and coal ash. No mine is worked for scandium alone.
in: Hidden in nickel, titanium and aluminium ores
steps.india: Present in the red mud from 8.2 Mt a year of alumina and in coal fly ash.

steps.title: Ride with another metal
steps.text: Scandium is recovered from the waste streams of other industries: the acid liquor of nickel laterite plants in the Philippines, the waste acid of titanium pigment plants in China and Canada, old tailings.
steps.india: NALCO has a fly-ash pilot (50 kg a day, August 2026) and plans a red-mud pilot.

steps.title: Extract
steps.text: Solvent extraction or ion-exchange resin pulls scandium out of a large volume of dilute acid. It is stripped, precipitated as oxalate and heated to give scandium oxide, a white powder. The world made about 80 tonnes of it in 2025.

steps.title: Make
steps.text: The oxide is converted to fluoride and reduced with calcium to metal, which is dissolved into aluminium as a master alloy with 2% scandium. Oxide is also blended into zirconia to make fuel-cell electrolyte.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: A fraction of a per cent of scandium makes aluminium far stronger and lets it be welded without losing strength, for aircraft and spacecraft. Scandia-stabilised zirconia is the electrolyte in solid-oxide fuel cells that power data centres and backup systems.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: None to speak of: too little is in use, and it is thinly spread through alloys.

sources.title: Takshashila, India Critical Minerals: scores, project records and capability notes (2026)
